utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would first like us to wait. Once and for all I would like my orders to be given before the accused is brought in, otherwise I find it a difficult way to operate. First of all, do all the interpreters hear? Is everybody ready? Does everybody hear me for this hearing of the initial appearance? Yes, I hear the French interpreters. Does the Prosecutor hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have no sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution hear now? Do you hear me now, Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you hear me now? Do you hear me, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I am afraid I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does Mr. Aleksovski hear me? THE DEFENDANT: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does the defence hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can begin the hearing, which is an initial appearance hearing, given the arrest and presence of one of the accused. I would first like the appearances for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Turn your microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, my name is Niemann. I appear with, on my left, Mr. Marchesiello. On my right is Mr. Meddegoda. We appear for the Prosecution in this matter, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could we have the appearance for the defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my name is Goran Mikulicic. I am the defence attorney of Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any kind of a warrant that you have with you? It is Mr. Mikulicic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are from the Zagreb bar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Be seated. I suppose that both the Prosecutor and the defence are prepared to move forward. I would like to recall the terms of the initial appearance hearing. The initial appearance of an accused is covered by a certain number of provisions which appear in the text, as well as by the International Criminal Tribunal's Statute and Rules. The Statute is covered in 20 and 21. Article 20 states that the Trial Chamber reads the indictment and makes sure that the rights of the accused have been respected, confirms that the accused has understood the indictment and instructs the accused to enter a plea. The Trial Chamber will then set a date for trial. In the same Statute there are a series of rights which have been provided for your client; among them the right to be informed as quickly as possible in a language which he understands in detail of the nature and cause of the charge against him, and to have time and facilities for the preparation of the defence, and there are other rights as well, which are made clear by your defence. These have to do with those steps which precede the hearing. Dealing more specifically with the initial hearing, which is the reason for our meeting today, the initial hearing of the accused is provided for in Rule 62 of the Rules. It is a relatively short rule, which says that the Trial Chamber -- the rights of the accused are respected, that he has the right to counsel, reads or has the indictment read to the accused in a language he speaks or understands, and satisfies itself that the accused understands the indictment. We will now do that. We will call the accused to enter a plea of "guilty" or "not guilty" on each count. Should the accused fail to do so, enter a plea of "not guilty" on his behalf and, last, if possible, one sets the date for the trial. If not possible, we set the date for whatever schedule can be done now in order to set up the schedule for the trial. I note, along with my colleagues, that the accused has an attorney. I would now like to turn to Mr. Mikulicic and first -- you may rise, sir. I would like you to assure us, assure the judges of Trial Chamber 1, that the accused has received a copy of the indictment and that it was read to him in a language which he understands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that my client has read the indictment and that he understood the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Has he himself read it, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you had the occasion to discuss it with him, although I do know that you only arrived this morning? Did you have the chance to speak about the indictment with your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, we have very few time to discuss the indictment, so pretty generally we discussed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. I will ask the Registrar to read the indictment and will again be translated for Mr. Aleksovski. I would like the Registrar to separate those parts which are relevant to Mr. Aleksovski. I give the floor to you, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The indictment contains the number IT-95-15-I and is dated 2nd November 1995. Indictment. Richard J Goldstone, Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, pursuant to his authority under Article 18 of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia ("The Statute of the Tribunal"), charges that: 1. Serious violations of international humanitarian law took place during the period of May 1992 to May 1993, when the armed forces of the Croatian Defence Council (hereinafter referred to as HVO) of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna (hereinafter referred to as HZ-HB) attacked the Muslim civilian population in the towns, villages and hamlets of the Lasva Valley area of Central Bosnia generally and specifically in the municipalitites of Vitez and Busovaca and the civilian population of the nearby city of Zenica, in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. 7. Zlatko Aleksovski, son of Tale and Eva (nee Stanko), was born on 8 January 1960 in Pakrac, Pakrac municipality, in the Republic of Croatia. He completed studies at the "Veljko Vlahovic" Faculty of Political Sciences, Department of Sociology, in Sarajevo on 28 September 1983. From 23 February 1987 he was employed as a counsellor at the "Zenica Correction House" until on or about 29 January 1993, when he left to become commander of the prison facility at Kaonik, near Busovaca. After May 1993 he left Kaonik to become the Head of the District HVO "Heliodrom" prison in Mostar, which was also under the administration of HZ-HB. 20. Zlatko Aleksovski was an official at the Zenica prison from 23 February 1987 until leaving to be the commander of the detention facility at Kaonik, near Busovaca, on or about 29 January 1993. He was in charge of Kaonik Prison and was in a position of superiority to everyone else in the camp. As commander, he met International Committee of the Red Cross (hereinafter referred to as ICRC) and European Community Monitoring Mission (hereinafter referred to as ECMM) officials and provided them with lists of detained persons and acknowledged his position of commander of the facility and his understanding of the Geneva Conventions in relation to the detention and treatment of prisoners in his charge. 21. Zlatko Aleksovski has demonstrated or exercised his control over the detention facility of Kaonik Prison in a variety of ways including, but not limited to, formal meetings with ICRC and ECMM officials, accepting the custody of arrested persons by HVO units, allowing the unlawful interrogation of detained persons and allowing them to be used for unlawful forced labour (digging trenches) and human shields. 31. From January 1993 until at least the end ... an international armed conflict and partial occupation existed in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. 22.2 All acts or omissions herein set forth as grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 (hereinafter "grave breaches"), recognised by Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal, occurred during that international armed conflict and partial occupation. 22.3 In each paragraph charging crimes against humanity, a crime recognised by Article 5 of the Statute of the Tribunal, the alleged acts or omissions were part of a widespread, large-scale or systematic attack directed against a civilian population, specifically the Bosnian Muslim population of the Lasva Valley region of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. 22.4 All of the victims referred to in the charges contained in this indictment were, at all relevant times, persons protected by the Geneva Conventions of 1949. 22.5 All of the accused in this indictment were required to abide by the mandate of the laws and customs governing the conduct of war, including the Geneva Conventions of 1949. 22.6 The general allegations contained in paragraphs 8 through to 22.5 are realleged and incorporated into each of the related charges set out below. Charges. 31. From January 1993 until at least the end of May 1993, Zlatko Aleksovski accepted hundreds of detained Bosnia Muslim civilians from the HVO or their agents into his custody at the detention facilities in Kaonik. The detainees were from a widespread area including, but not exclusive to, Vitez and Busovaca municipalitites. Many of the detainees under his control were subjected to inhumane treatment, including, but not limited to, excessive and cruel interrogation, physical and psychological harm, forced labour (digging trenches), in hazardous circumstances, being used as human shields and some were murdered or otherwise killed. Counts 8-10. Grave Breaches and Violation of the Laws or Customs of War. Unlawful treatment of Bosnian Muslim detainees. 37. Dario Cordic, Tihofil Blaskic, Mario Cerkez, Ivan Santic, Pero Skopljak and Zlatko Aleksovski, between 1 January and 31 May 1993, and as otherwise described in paragraphs 23 and 26-31 of this indictment, all of which are incorporated in full herein, individually, and in concert with others, planned, instigated, ordered or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation or execution of the unlawful treatment of Bosnian Muslim detainees in the Lasva Valley area of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and, or in the alternative, knew, or had reason to know, that subordinates were about to do the same, or had done so, and failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish the perpetrators thereof. By these acts and omissions Dario Kordic, Tihofil Blaskic, Mario Cerkez, Ivan Santic, Pero Skopljak and Zlatko Aleksovski committed: Count 8: a GRAVE BREACH as recognised by Articles 2(b) (inhuman treatment), 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal; Count 9: a GRAVE BREACH as recognised by Articles 2(c) (wilfully causing great suffering or serious injury to body or health), 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal; Count 10: a VIOLATION OF THE LAWS OR CUSTOMS OF WAR (outrages upon the personal dignity) as recognised by Articles 3, 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. This indictment was amended by a Decision of 22 November 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Registrar. Thank you for reading this. Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski, would you rise, please? Would you state your name, your first name, any relations that you have, any other identifying characteristics, your profession today? We are listening to you. THE DEFENDANT: My name is Zlatko Aleksovski, the son of Tale Aleksovski. My mother's name is Eva Stanko. I was born on 8 January 1960 in Pakrac in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You studied political science; is that correct? What is your profession today? THE DEFENDANT: Until I was indicted, I worked as Manager of the District Court in Busovaca. I graduated in political sciences in Sarajevo, Department of Sociology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksovski, you are being prosecuted under the indictment which has been drafted by the Prosecutor against you, which explains the reasons for your arrest and presence here today. You have heard those parts of the Statute which relate to you. You heard the indictment. Your counsel has explained it to you. I would like you to tell me whether you understood what was read, whether it was read to you in a language which is yours, and for you to tell me as well whether you plead "guilty" or "not guilty" to each of the three counts in the indictment, two having to do with graves breaches of the Geneva Convention, and one count of violation of the laws and customs of war. First question: do you confirm that you read the indictment, read it in a language which you understand? THE DEFENDANT: Yes, I have read the indictment in a language I understand. That was last night, when the Registrar gave it to me in the original officially, because that was the first time I received it officially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, you can with all lucidity state whether or not you are pleading "guilty" or "not guilty". This is the question which myself and the other judges are asking you. The indictment provides under Count 8 grave breach of the Geneva Convention recognised by Articles 2(b) (inhuman treatment) and 7(1) and 7(3), referring to individual responsibility. As to Count 8, serious breach of the Geneva Convention, do you plead "guilty" or "not guilty"? THE DEFENDANT: Your Honour, I have understood what the Registrar read as well as this count that you are referring to. I have read it but I deny all culpability for the charges and I do not feel responsible. Therefore I plead "not guilty".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This will be recorded in the transcripts of this hearing by the Registrar. As to Count 9, which also relates to a serious breach of the Geneva Convention, specifically Article 2(c) of the Statute, the fact of having intentionally caused serious harm to the person, whether psychological or physical, under Article 7(1) and 7(3), do you take the same position, that you plead "not guilty"? THE DEFENDANT: I confirm what I have already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. This will also be recorded. Last, having to do with Count Number 10, the violation of laws and customs of war, those having to do with causing great suffering or serious injury to body or health, outrages on the person's dignity, as recognised by Articles 3, 7(1) and 7(3), as to this count, what is your position? Do you plead "guilty" or "not guilty" to that count? THE DEFENDANT: As I said a moment ago, I plead "not guilty" to all the counts. I consider myself absolutely innocent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This will also be recorded in the transcript of today's hearing. You may be seated, Mr. Aleksovski. THE DEFENDANT: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would now like to turn to the Prosecution. Starting today, a certain number of required time periods begin to run. The first obligation, which is the Prosecutor's, pursuant to Rule 66 of the Rules, is that, starting today, Prosecution, the Prosecutor must make available to the defence, as soon as practicable after the initial appearance of the accused, copies of the supporting material which accompanied the indictment when confirmation was sought, as well as all prior statements obtained by the Prosecutor for the accused or from Prosecution witnesses. The final version of this statement, translations of this material must be made into the language of the accused, which he understands. Turning to the Prosecutor, where are you? What time period are you giving yourself in order to disclose all these documents to the defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, the position of the Prosecution on this matter is that we require, with your Honour's leave, time to at least consult with the principal witnesses that are disclosed in the material, in order to just ascertain whether there are any security matters which we would need to address in the event of discovery under that provision. We are embarking on that exercise forthwith, and we will endeavour to make discovery in as short a practicable time as possible. Subject to the convenience of the court, we would today be seeking an adjournment of the matter until -- for a status conference, and I think that we would be in a much better position to inform the court of our progress in this matter in a period of three to four weeks. In that time we would hope to have progressed the issue of discovery, if not in whole, in part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I understand that you cannot disclose all of the documents right now, but do you already have documents which you can disclose to the defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not in a position right at this moment, your Honour, to say exactly what we can disclose and what we cannot, but my understanding is that there is some material that we believe we could make available in a very short time. We are working on that and will endeavour to make that material available as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Since Mr. Aleksovski was supposed to be at the Tribunal several weeks ago already -- I believe that the International Criminal Tribunal has been expecting him ever since the indictment was issued, that is November 1995, if I can recall -- again I recall the date, November 1995. However, Prosecutor, you do intend, do you not, to set a date quickly? . Could you give us a period, amount of time, how much you need for disclosing the documents? If I am insisting on this, it is because experience in other cases leads me to think that very often a great deal of time is needed in order to get going before a trial can begin. The texts provide for our setting the date of the trial as of today. Of course, we will not be able to do so, but in so far as Mr. Aleksovski was supposed to be here since December, I do suppose that certain documents already could be communicated. If I ask you this, it is because you know and the defence knows as well that you have 60 days starting from today to decide whether you will file preliminary motions or not within the scope of this trial. Today we will set the date for the end of that period, which will be 28th June, but perhaps it would be proper for you to say to us what period of time you expect to be able to give to us a certain number of documents. You understand my concern, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Precisely, your Honour. Indeed, we will be endeavouring to make available material as soon as we possibly can. With respect to witness statements, there are genuine and sensitive concerns that we have, which we just simply need to check out. It is not a question of just not being in a position to alternately discover it. It is just a question of do we need to take steps in order to afford protection, if that is required. Indeed, it would be remiss of us, your Honour, if we did not at least pursue that exercise. These things, because you need to locate various witnesses and speak to them in order to ascertain their position, do take some time. That is why I suggested a period of one month, which I thought would be reasonable for this purpose. There is other material, which is not affected in this way, and I would imagine, your Honours, that this could be made available in a shorter period than that one month period. I would expect that we would be embarking on the process of discovery within the next ten days, when we have sorted the material which we feel can be readily separated from the body of the material which was discovered -- which was made available for the whole of the indictment. Your Honours are aware, of course, that this indictment relates only in part to the accused, Mr. Aleksovski, and there is a whole lot, a mass of material which relates to other accused, which may not fall within the scope of the Rule, but it is not our intention to delay this exercise. It is not our intention to be difficult in respect of discovery. It is our intention to be as open and to be as efficient as possible in making this material available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Prosecutor. If I have understood you well, from now -- ten days from now -- Mr. Triscos, about ten days the Prosecutor has said. That would be 10th May. Shall we say 10th May? From now until 10th May you will be able to submit a series of documents, which do not directly require protection of witnesses, also witness statements, hoping that these will be corroborated, and that protection measures will not represent an insurmountable problem, or simply other declarations, which need not be witness statements, pieces of evidence, agendas, various other documents. Therefore, we are taking note that by May 10th you will have disclosed to the defence a series of documents, and that within one month, that is by the beginning of June, we can meet again to see what progress you have made with your witnesses, which measures you wish to take, protection measures, for your witnesses, and perhaps we will also know what the preliminary motions will be. Therefore, Mr. Prosecutor, by May 10th a certain number of documents will be submitted to the defence. We will not specify which documents those will be, and then within a time period of one month we should meet again to see what steps the Prosecutor requires regarding protection of witness, and the defence also can convey to us their first observations regarding the documents which will be disclosed to them by May 10th. I now ask Mr. Mikulicic -- thank you, Mr. Prosecutor -- Mr Mikulicic, considering what the Prosecutor has said, I would like to see whether this planning is acceptable to you. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I am allowed to use my own native language, it will be much easier for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you have permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (In interpretation): I wish to welcome the court ruling, fixing a deadline for disclosure of documents. The defence would like, most of all, to have all the documents that are referred to in the indictment, to have insight into them as soon as possible, for it is in the interest of the defence for this trial to be efficient and effective so as not to have any unnecessary delays. Therefore, the defence agrees to this deadline of 10th May for the submission of documents, as well as the date for another hearing of the Trial Chamber regarding progress made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. So if you are agreeable, we will bear in mind and take note in the minutes of this initial appearance hearing that by 10th May the Prosecutor will disclose a number of documents in conformity with Article 66. On the other hand, we will set a date for a status conference, which will be held in about one month, and which would allow us to establish how we stand with the files. That will be halfway of the period of 60 days allowed for preliminary motions. The end of those 60 days is 29th June. Therefore, I propose that we meet -- let me see. Let me consult my colleagues for a minute. (Pause.) Very well. I propose that we meet again on Wednesday, June 4th, the morning or the afternoon, depending on your other obligations. Do you prefer the afternoon, Mr. Mikulicic? Is that easier for you in view of the air transport and other considerations? Do you prefer the morning or the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. An afternoon hearing would suit the defence more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will give you the time, but in any event a status conference will be held on June 4th in the afternoon. Mr. Prosecutor, will that give you enough time regarding the question of witness protection? Is that date suitable?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is suitable, your Honour, so that the Prosecution can be in a position to report on where it is in terms of any requests it might be making with respect to witness protection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Registrar? (Pause.) I have a small correction to make. The Registry have noted that in mid-June we will still be involved with the Celebici case and that on Fridays there are no hearings. Therefore, perhaps the status conference could be fixed for Friday, June 6th, at the end of the morning. Would that suit you? Would that give you enough time to get here, Mr. Mikulicic? About 11 o'clock on June 6th?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I will adjust my timetable to the needs and decision of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, Friday, 11 o'clock, June 6th, is it acceptable to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is acceptable, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. In that case the Tribunal has decided that, first of all, by 10th May all the documents under Rule 66 which are not covered by special protection will be disclosed to the defence. Secondly, the Trial Chamber decides that on Friday, June 6th, at 11 o'clock, a status conference will be held, which will have a two-fold object. First, the Prosecutor will present the results of all its enquiries that have taken place over more than a month, that is during five weeks, whether he will keep certain witnesses, reject them or ask for special protection measures. Also we will hear the views of Mr. Mikulicic on the basis of the documents he has seen, whether he will have any preliminary motions to make within the delay of 60 days, but that date will have to be fixed on that occasion and let it not be delayed beyond the deadline. At that point we will fix the date for the beginning of trial. I now turn my attention to Mr. Aleksovski. Do you have any statement to make, Mr. Aleksovski, on the basis of what you have heard regarding the dates and the schedules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have nothing to state at this moment. I have followed carefully the proceedings and I agree with all that has been decided. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You may be seated. Thank you. The meeting is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: --ooOoo--
